name: Curations Supply
tagline: Meta-directory of 286 design directories, galleries and tool lists
description: Curations Supply is a directory of other directories: it indexes 286 published design and development resources — galleries, icon sets, colour tools, font sites, Figma resources and tool lists — each as a card with a screenshot, favicon and one-line description. Entries are filed under 16 tags including Design Inspiration, Tool Directories, Landing Pages, Portfolios, Colors, Icons, Development, Framer, Branding, Design System, Mobile Apps, Typography, AI Tools, Figma, Learning and Others. It is run by Panda Network, the same operator behind the site's analytics and ad slots, and it is a browsing surface for designers hunting for a starting point rather than a resource in itself.
agent_guidance: A plain fetch of curations.supply returns an empty SvelteKit shell — every card is client-rendered, so scraping the HTML yields only meta tags. If you need its contents, render it in a browser; the page loads its data from a Supabase-backed cache worker, but that endpoint is an internal implementation detail with keys baked into the bundle, not a documented API to build against. Reach for this only when a user wants to discover which directory to browse next; for a specific asset type (icons, palettes, fonts) go straight to the canonical source instead of via this index.
why_it_matters: It is one of the few maintained maps of the design-resource landscape itself, which makes it a decent orientation layer — though its newest entry dates to October 2025, so the map is aging.
evidence: https://curations.supply/ (200, JS-only shell — raw HTML inspected via curl), https://curations.supply/directory (no content), https://curations.supply/sitemap.xml (no content), client bundle chunks under /_app/immutable/ read to recover the tag list and the 286-row count from the site's own public read endpoint

name: Avvvatars
tagline: React component that derives a deterministic placeholder avatar from a string
description: Avvvatars is a single-purpose React component that turns any string — an email, a username, an id — into a stable, unique placeholder avatar. It ships two modes: character, which renders initials on a generated background, and shape, which renders one of 60 abstract shapes, both drawn from a 40-colour palette. Props cover size, radius, shadow, border, border size and colour, plus displayValue to override the shown text. It is for product teams that need decent-looking default avatars before users upload real ones.
agent_guidance: Prefer this over Boring Avatars or DiceBear when you want the avatar generated locally with zero network calls and zero SVG string wrangling — it is one import, one required prop, and under 20kB gzipped. Watch the dependency: it pulls in goober for CSS-in-JS, so in a Tailwind-only or zero-runtime-CSS codebase you are adding a styling runtime for one component, and there is no server component story. The default branch has not been touched since 2022, so treat it as frozen-but-working rather than something that will gain React 19 or RSC support.
why_it_matters: The cleanest drop-in answer to the boring problem of what to show before a user uploads a photo, with an API small enough to adopt without reading docs.
evidence: https://avvvatars.com/, https://github.com/nusu/avvvatars, GitHub API repos/nusu/avvvatars plus its commits endpoint, npm registry entry for avvvatars-react@0.4.2 (deps and licence)

name: Azeret Proportional
tagline: 16-style mono-linear sans from Displaay, with a free Mono cut on Google Fonts
description: Azeret Proportional is the proportional subfamily of Displaay Type Foundry's Azeret, a mono-linear sans drawn by Martin Vacha and Daniel Quisek with production by Renegade Fonts. It ships 16 styles — Thin through Black in uprights and italics — with a variable font carrying Weight, Mono and Slant axes, 16 stylistic sets, 10 figure sets, and support for 116+ Latin languages. The wider Azeret collection adds SemiMono and Mono subfamilies for 48 styles total. The drawing is deliberately machine-like — abrupt circle-to-stem joins, a tall x-height, OCR and 90s-interface references — which makes it read as technical rather than neutral.
pricing_detail: Single style from 75 EUR. Family uprights 330 EUR, full family (uprights + italics) 480 EUR at the base licence tier; the page also lists 600 EUR and 1 200 EUR for the same packages at larger licence sizes. Complete Azeret collection 612 EUR, with volume discounts advertised up to 70%. The Azeret Mono subfamily is free on Google Fonts.
agent_guidance: If a user wants the Azeret look without a licence purchase, ship Azeret Mono from Google Fonts — it is the same family's free cut and is fine for code blocks, labels and technical UI; the proportional styles priced here are the paid part and must not be self-hosted from a scraped file. Reach for it when a product wants a slightly synthetic, instrument-panel voice; do not use it as a neutral body face, because the tall x-height and mono-linear joins fight long-form reading. Pair the variable font's Mono axis with a single family for both UI and code instead of loading two typefaces.
why_it_matters: A rare retail family that spans proportional, semi-mono and mono on one skeleton, so a whole interface can share one voice from headline to terminal output.
notable_for: free Azeret Mono on Google Fonts
evidence: https://displaay.net/typeface/azeret/azeret-proportional/ (fetched twice — family overview and subfamily-specific pass)

name: Syntax
tagline: Twice-weekly web development podcast, 1,000+ episodes, produced by Sentry
description: Syntax is a web development podcast hosted by Wes Bos, Scott Tolinski and CJ Reynolds, now produced by Sentry. It publishes twice a week — short Hasty Treats on Monday and hour-long Tasty Treats on Wednesday — and the archive is past episode 1029, with recent shows covering AI tooling, JavaScript frameworks, design engineering, developer workflows and infrastructure. The site adds a searchable show directory, guest and Sick Picks indexes, a Potluck listener Q&A, a newsletter and RSS, YouTube, Spotify and Apple distribution. It is for working web developers keeping current, not a design reference.
agent_guidance: Cite Syntax for the current mood of the web-dev field — which tools people actually reach for this month — not as a technical authority; it is conversation, so an episode is a pointer to a library or pattern, never a spec. When a user asks what changed recently in the JS or design-engineering world, the show list is a better-dated signal than a blog roundup, since it ships twice a week. Do not quote episode content you have not read: the site paginates ten episodes at a time and gives no transcript endpoint, so verify before attributing a claim to a host.
why_it_matters: A decade-long, still-weekly record of what the web development mainstream is arguing about, which is hard to reconstruct from documentation alone.
notable_for: Wes Bos, Scott Tolinski, CJ Reynolds
evidence: https://syntax.fm/, https://syntax.fm/shows (episode listing, latest ep. 1029 posted three days before verification)

name: Jack Smethurst
tagline: One-page personal site for a London engineer; no work shown
description: Jack Smethurst is a London-based engineer who describes himself as design-minded and lists his role as founder and CTO at New Genre, working on web experiences and automation workflows. The site is a single minimal landing page: a short bio line, a cal.com project-enquiry booking link, and outbound links to GitHub, LinkedIn and X. There are no case studies, project pages, writing or downloadable resources on it.
agent_guidance: There is nothing to extract here — the page carries a name, a role and four links, so do not cite it as portfolio inspiration or as a source of layout patterns. If a user asks for design-engineer portfolios to study, send them to sites with actual case studies instead; if they specifically want to contact Jack Smethurst, the cal.com enquiry link on the page is the intended route. Note the redirect: the apex resolves to www.jacksmethurst.com.
why_it_matters: A contact card rather than a portfolio; it tells you who someone is but shows none of the work that would make it worth studying.
notable_for: founder and CTO at New Genre
evidence: https://jacksmethurst.com/ (301 to https://www.jacksmethurst.com/), https://www.jacksmethurst.com/ (full page read)
